benchmark.short_description: Colored-grid abstraction tasks that test few-shot rule induction, not memorized facts, language fluency, or school math.
benchmark.status_evidence: ARC-AGI-1 remains useful as a historical abstraction benchmark, but the official ARC Prize leaderboard generated on 2026-07-23 lists multiple verified systems above 95% on the ARC-AGI-1 semi-private axis, including GPT-5.6 Sol at 97.5%. ARC Prize launched ARC-AGI-2 because ARC-AGI-1 had become too brute-forceable and less discriminative for frontier systems.

contamination.mitigation: The public train and evaluation tasks are fully available on GitHub. ARC Prize later introduced semi-private and private evaluation sets for leaderboard and competition testing, but ARC-AGI-1 still has a fixed, old private pool and a long history of submissions. Contamination risk is therefore high for public-set scores and medium-to-high even for public leaderboard comparisons unless the split and testing policy are clear.

human_baseline.note: The official ARC Prize leaderboard lists a Human Panel score of 98% on the ARC-AGI-1 semi-private axis. Older public-page summaries also report lower average-human estimates; the sidebar uses the current official leaderboard value.

benchmark.statistical_note: The public evaluation split has 400 tasks, but ARC Prize leaderboard scores use the semi-private axis and competitions may use private splits. Treat scores as comparable only when the split, attempt budget, model/system type, and cost budget are named.
benchmark.metric_primary: task success rate on the evaluation split (%)

benchmark.name: BIG-Bench Hard
benchmark.short_description: 23 BIG-Bench tasks where models trailed humans — the benchmark that proved chain-of-thought prompting works, then fell to the reasoning-model era.
benchmark.status_evidence: Frontier and reasoning-tuned models exceed ~90% on the 23-task average and are near-perfect on many individual tasks; the reasoning-model era made BBH trivial. Google DeepMind built BBEH (2025) — replacing each task with a harder counterpart — precisely because BBH stopped discriminating at the top.

contamination.mitigation: Inherits BIG-bench's public tasks and its widely-ignored canary GUID. BBH's popularity made it especially likely to appear in pretraining and instruction-tuning data, and there is no refreshed variant. Its high contamination risk is a direct reason BBEH was built with fresh tasks.

human_baseline.note: Average human-rater performance across the 23 tasks in the original paper; the best (max) human rater averaged ~94.4%. BBH tasks were selected precisely as the BIG-Bench tasks where prior models fell below the 67.7% average-rater line. (Canonical Table 1 values from the paper.)

benchmark.statistical_note: 6,511 examples across 23 unequally-sized tasks; because the aggregate is an unweighted task average, a small task moves the number as much as a large one. Now that the mean is saturated, per-task scores — not the 23-task average — are where any remaining signal lives.
benchmark.metric_primary: exact-match accuracy, averaged over 23 tasks (%)

benchmark.name: Humanity's Last Exam
benchmark.short_description: ~2,500 expert-written questions across 100+ subjects, each filtered to stump frontier models — designed to be the final closed-ended academic benchmark.
benchmark.status_evidence: The clearest active benchmark on the wiki. Launch scores were single digits (GPT-4o 3.3%, o1 9.1%, DeepSeek-R1 9.4%, no tools); the current no-tools frontier is ~38% (Gemini 3 Pro, Nov 2025) — a steep climb but a long way from solved. Given the 'last exam' thesis, saturation here would mean closed-ended academic testing has run out of headroom entirely, so 'what replaces it' points toward open-ended, agentic, and interactive evaluation rather than a harder Q&A set. Note: tool-augmented and agent scores run much higher and are tracked separately (see Timeline).

contamination.mitigation: The strongest mitigation design catalogued on the wiki so far: alongside the public ~2,500-question set, CAIS/Scale hold a PRIVATE set of questions used to detect benchmark-specific overfitting by comparing a model's public vs private performance — a static-but-audited design. The public set is gated on HuggingFace (accept an agreement; users are asked not to re-share or re-upload). This does not make it leak-proof — the public questions are discussed online and the failure-filter selected for 2024-frontier blind spots — but the private audit catches the crudest gaming, which is why the risk is medium rather than high despite a fully static public set.

human_baseline.note: No human baseline — and here the concept itself breaks down. HLE spans 100+ expert subjects from classics to rocket engineering; no single human could sit the whole exam, so an aggregate 'human score' is undefined in principle, not merely unmeasured. This differs from SimpleQA, where a human COULD take the test but the score would mostly measure Googling: HLE is superhuman in BREADTH by construction. The only meaningful human reference is per-question — each was solved by the domain expert who wrote it — which is exactly why the benchmark exists: to test whether one model can match the union of many human specialists.

benchmark.statistical_note: ~2,500 questions give a workable aggregate CI (±~2pt at 40%), but two non-sampling caveats dominate. First, scores move FAST — a published number is often stale within months (single digits to ~38% in under a year), so always read HLE figures with their date and this page's last_updated. Second, the number is meaningless without its CONFIGURATION: no-tools vs tool-augmented vs multi-agent 'heavy' modes differ by tens of points on the same model (see Timeline). Read accuracy beside calibration error, and never compare across tool settings.
benchmark.metric_primary: accuracy, no tools (%)
benchmark.judge_model: GPT-4o (gpt-4o-2024-08-06, structured decoding) checks whether a model's answer is equivalent to the reference for the 80% short-answer questions. Judge model/version drift makes scores across grader versions not strictly comparable — pin the grader.
